title: {{NAME}} and the Thunderfoot Tournament
moral: The fastest player on the pitch is the one who makes everyone around them better.

pages.content: The Thunderfoot Tournament had been running for longer than anyone remembered, held every season in the Great Basin, a bowl-shaped valley so large that clouds formed inside it. The pitch was older than kingdoms, its grass a prehistoric variety that grew back within hours of being cut and had a springiness underfoot that made you feel, with each step, as if the ground were helping you forward. The teams were unlike any {{NAME}} had competed against. There were dinosaurs of every variety playing in organised leagues, the quick-footed Velociraptors of the Canyon Scrubs who communicated during play in a language of rapid, intricate clicks, the Ankylosaur defenders of the Iron Valley who were slow but essentially immovable, and the Brachiosaurus of the Cloud Meadow team, who played from such a height that their perspective on the game was, quite literally, different from everyone else's. The fairies served as referees and linespeople, too quick for any protest to outrun them. {{NAME}} stood at the Basin rim and looked down at all of it with the feeling of having opened a door to a room he had not known existed.

pages.content: {{NAME}}'s team, the Ferncliff United, was an assortment that did not, at first inspection, inspire obvious confidence. His co-striker was a young Velociraptor named Cob, who was enormously powerful but who had the unfortunate habit of overthinking everything to the point of paralysis. Their goalkeeper was a short-necked Plesiosaur named Dip, who had come up from the river for the occasion and who kept getting distracted by interesting clouds. The team captain was a fairy named Wren, barely visible unless she held still, who made up for her size with a tactical intelligence so sharp it could have cut glass. She hovered before the team in the dugout and delivered the pre-match briefing in a voice like a tiny trumpet. 'Cob, stop thinking,' she said. 'Dip, no clouds. {{NAME}}, you will play the spaces between the Velociraptor clicks. They communicate right before they move. Listen for it and you will be ahead of them every time.' {{NAME}} had not considered that you could eavesdrop on a dinosaur's tactical language. He was beginning to feel that this tournament had a great deal to teach him.

pages.content: Wren was right about the clicks. The Velociraptor midfield were brilliant, the fastest passing unit {{NAME}} had ever faced, their exchanges so rapid and precise they were almost invisible to the eye. But the soft double-click that preceded a through ball was unmistakeable once you knew to listen for it, like a key turning in a lock. The first time {{NAME}} moved on the click, cutting across a pass that had not yet been made, the Velociraptor midfielder stopped completely and regarded him with unsettling amber eyes. Then it made a sound that Wren, streaking past, identified as a dinosaur compliment. Cob found his rhythm too. {{NAME}} stopped calling for the ball and started simply running the right line at the right moment, and Cob, unburdened of making a decision, simply passed to where {{NAME}} was heading, and the release of thinking seemed to dissolve all of Cob's paralysis. The Ankylosaur defenders were another matter: vast, armoured, immovable. 'Don't go through them,' said {{NAME}} at the break. 'Go over. Chip ball, every time.' Dip, who had finally stopped looking at clouds, turned out to have hands that could hold the lowest trajectory chip pass anyone had ever seen.

pages.content: The match-winning moment came from the last person any of them expected. Wren had been managing the game from above, calling adjustments with her tiny trumpet voice, when an Ankylosaur's armoured tail swing caught the ball and deflected it wildly toward the Ferncliff goal. Dip lunged, but the angle was impossible. {{NAME}} was too far. Cob turned, gauged the trajectory, stopped thinking, and threw himself at it with a diving header that shook the ancient pitch when he landed. The ball went straight and true into the opposing net. The impact of Cob's landing sent a tremor through the ground that the fairies, every single one of them, performed a simultaneous loop-the-loop in the air as if the earth itself had thrown them upward. Cob lay on the pitch face-down for a moment, then raised one enormous thumb at {{NAME}}. The clouds inside the Great Basin basin chose this moment to produce a brief warm rain, which fell on everyone equally and seemed entirely appropriate. Wren landed on {{NAME}}'s shoulder and said nothing, which was more eloquent than her entire tactical briefing.

pages.content: After the tournament, the Ferncliff team gathered on the springy prehistoric grass as the basin emptied. Cob ate a small tree with the calm efficiency of an Velociraptor who has earned it. Dip sat in the rain puddles, very happy. The Velociraptor midfielder from the opposing team found {{NAME}} and clicked three precise times, then walked away. Wren translated: 'It said you play like something old.' {{NAME}} wasn't sure whether to be flattered. 'In dinosaur terms,' said Wren, 'there is no higher compliment.' The basin was quiet now, the prehistoric grass already springing back from the match, unbothered and patient. {{NAME}} ran his fingers through it as he walked toward the exit, feeling its energy push back gently against his palm. He felt full of something that was bigger than just winning. He thought about Cob discovering something in himself in the moment he stopped thinking, and Dip finally watching the right thing, and Wren's silence that meant everything. At the exit of the Great Basin, he turned once to look back. He was almost certain the grass was still moving, in a slow pattern, as if the ancient pitch were breathing.
